title: Third Normal Form
description: Third Normal Form is the 1992 album from Procedural Byts: twelve tracks of grunge and alternative metal about how data is stored, linked and kept true. Nyble sings lead and plays bass, Qword plays lead guitar, Wyrd unplugs the synths for a distorted church-sale organ, and Bytes plays drums and sings backup. SQL queries, entity-relationship design, primary and foreign keys, joins, aggregation, update anomalies, normalization, NULL, indexes, transactions and crash recovery. Written after a tour where every member kept their own copy of the setlist and no two ever matched. Null finally gets a song of its own. Play loud. Store it once.
tagline: The 1992 grunge album from Procedural Byts: a databases course in twelve songs, and the end of the four-setlist problem.
lineup: Still a four-piece, now unplugged. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass guitar. Qword plays lead guitar. Wyrd plays organ instead of synths. Bytes plays drums and sings backup.

members.name: Nyble
members.bio: Four bits, and the keeper of the one true setlist. Nyble sings lead on every song and plays bass, and her copy of the setlist is now the only one that exists.

members.name: Qword
members.bio: Sixty-four bits and, as of 1992, forbidden from shredding. Qword spent the year learning to play three notes slowly, with feeling. It was agony. It sounds great.

members.name: Wyrd
members.bio: Thirty-two bits, and no synthesizers for the first time since joining the band. Wyrd found an organ at a church sale and plays it through an amp with a broken speaker, which Wyrd insists is part of the sound.

members.name: Bytes
members.bio: Eight bits, and the owner of the setlist that still listed songs from 1979. Bytes plays drums, sings backup, and chose ID number one for himself.

members.name: Null
members.bio: Finally has a song named after it. When asked whether it was equal to itself, the duck said nothing, which is the correct answer.

story.heading: The Setlist Problem
paragraphs: By 1992, nobody wanted synthesizers or shred solos anymore. Wyrd unplugged the entire synth rig, bought an old organ at a church sale, and played it through an amp with a broken speaker. Qword was told that guitar solos were over and spent the year learning to play three notes, slowly, with feeling.

On the Q.E.D. tour, every member had kept their own copy of the setlist. Nyble’s had the songs in one order and Qword’s in another. Wyrd had renamed two of the songs. Bytes’s copy still listed songs from 1979. When Nyble changed a song, only her copy changed, and every night somebody played the wrong one.
It got worse. They couldn’t add a new song to the set until it had a show to be played at. When they dropped a song, Bytes erased it from his copy, along with the only record of what key it was in.

So they made an album about fixing it. One setlist, kept in one place, with every song stored once and given a number. Every other list refers to the songs by number, so if you change a song, you change it once.
Null got a song of its own, and the band asked the duck the obvious question: are you equal to yourself? The duck said nothing. According to the database, that is the correct answer.
The last thing they recorded was Commit. Afterwards they threw three of the four setlists in the bin and kept one. Nobody has played the wrong song since.

cover_sub: The 1992 album. Recorded in a basement, in the rain, with the synths unplugged.

songs.title: Select All

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Tell me what you want and not the way to go,
Name the columns and the table, that’s all I need to know.
Where the year is ninety-two and the sky is full of rain,
The optimizer picks the path and you never feel the pain.

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Select all! (From the table!)
Select all! (If you’re able!)
Where the rows are true, I’ll bring them home,
Select star, and you’re never alone!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Order by the date and the newest ones come first,
Distinct will drop the doubles when the duplicates are cursed.
You say the what, I find the how, a plan inside my head,
Declarative and simple, and it’s everything you said.

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Select! (What you want!) From! (Where it lives!)
Where! (What it gives!)

parts.label: Organ solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Wyrd’s first solo without a synthesizer: a distorted church organ through a broken speaker. It doesn’t play every note in the scale, only the ones that match the condition.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Select all! (From the table!)
Select all! (If you’re able!)
Where the rows are true, I’ll bring them home,
Select star, and you’re never alone!

songs.note: The first song recorded without synthesizers in seven years. Wyrd played it on a church-sale organ.
songs.lesson: SQL is declarative: you say what you want, not how to get it. SELECT names the columns, FROM names the table, WHERE gives the condition rows must meet, ORDER BY sorts and DISTINCT removes duplicates. The database’s query optimizer works out the fastest way to get the answer.

songs.title: Entity, Relationship

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Draw a box for every thing, a band, a song, a show,
Each box an entity with attributes it needs to know.
Draw a diamond for the ties, a band plays many songs,
A line from box to diamond tells you where it all belongs.

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Entity! Relationship!
Draw it before you build!
Entity! Relationship!
Every promise filled!
Turn the boxes into tables and the lines into keys,
Entity, relationship, and the data’s at ease!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A table is a relation, rows and columns in a grid,
Every row a tuple, every column what it did.
No order to the rows, just a set of facts that hold,
The schema is the shape of it, the story that it’s told.

parts.label: Bridge
lines: One to one! (A band, a name!)
One to many! (A band, its songs!)
Many to many! (Songs and shows, where everything belongs!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword’s first grunge solo, and the first time in history Qword has played only three notes: one for the entity, one for the relationship, one for the other entity. It was agony. It sounds great.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Entity! Relationship!
Draw it before you build!
Entity! Relationship!
Every promise filled!
Turn the boxes into tables and the lines into keys,
Entity, relationship, and the data’s at ease!

songs.note: Drawn on a napkin first. The napkin is on the back cover.
songs.lesson: Entity-relationship modeling designs a database before you build it: entities (things, like bands, songs and shows) with attributes, and relationships between them with cardinalities: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. In the relational model, a table is a relation: a set of rows (tuples) with named columns, and the schema describes its shape.

songs.title: Primary Key

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Two rows that look the same and I can’t tell which is which,
Same name, same town, same birthday, and the data’s in a ditch.
Give every row a value that no other row can claim,
A primary key, and the key is your name!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Primary key! (Unique!)
Primary key! (Never null!)
One for every row, and every row has one,
Primary key, and the search is done!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A candidate is any set of columns that’s unique,
Pick one to be the primary, the one you’ll always seek.
Never let it change and never leave it blank,
It’s the anchor in the river and the rock beside the bank!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Who are you? (Number one!)
Who are you? (Number two!)
No two the same, and no one without a clue!

parts.label: Bass solo: Nyble
parts.desc: Nyble plays one short riff for each member of the band, and no two riffs are the same. Each one tells you exactly who it’s about.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Primary key! (Unique!)
Primary key! (Never null!)
One for every row, and every row has one,
Primary key, and the search is done!

songs.note: Every member got an ID number during these sessions. Bytes is number one. He chose it.
songs.lesson: A primary key uniquely identifies each row in a table: its values must be unique and never NULL. A candidate key is any minimal set of columns that is unique, and one of them is chosen as the primary key. Keys should never change, which is why many designs simply use a generated ID number.

songs.title: Referential Integrity

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: My table holds the songs and your table holds the shows,
Your row says song number seven, and that’s how the linking goes.
A foreign key points over to a key that’s really there,
Delete the song it points to and it’s pointing at the air!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Referential integrity! (Point to something real!)
Referential integrity! (That’s the deal!)
No reference to nowhere, no orphans in the night,
Referential integrity, and the links are right!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Try to add a show that plays a song that doesn’t exist,
The database refuses, it’s a constraint upon the list.
Delete a song that’s still in use and it will stop you cold,
Or cascade it all away, if that’s what you were told!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Orphan row! (No parent!) Dangling! (Nowhere to go!)
Cascade! (Delete them all!) Restrict! (Tell them no!)

parts.label: Organ solo: Wyrd
parts.desc: Every organ phrase Wyrd plays answers one that Qword has already played. When Qword stops, Wyrd can’t continue, because there’s nothing left to refer to.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Referential integrity! (Point to something real!)
Referential integrity! (That’s the deal!)
No reference to nowhere, no orphans in the night,
Referential integrity, and the links are right!

songs.note: The first song where the band’s setlists started pointing at each other instead of copying each other.
songs.lesson: A foreign key is a column that refers to the primary key of another table, linking rows together. Referential integrity means every foreign key points to a row that really exists. The database rejects inserts that would break that, and when a referenced row is deleted it can refuse, cascade the delete, or set the reference to NULL.

songs.title: Join Me

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: You’ve got the songs and I’ve got the shows,
Separate tables, separate rows.
Match them on the column where our numbers agree,
Put us side by side, and that’s the you and me!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Join me! (Inner join!)
Only where we match!
Join me! (Outer join!)
Keep the ones without a catch!
The left side and the right side together on the line,
Join me, join me, and your rows will meet mine!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: An inner join keeps only the pairs where both are there,
A left join keeps all of mine, with nulls in empty air.
Forget the join condition and you’ll pair up every one,
A cross product of everything, and the query’s never done!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: On! (The key!) Where! (The rule!)
Forget the on, and you’re a fool!

parts.label: Guitar and organ duet: Qword and Wyrd
parts.desc: Qword and Wyrd play two different melodies at the same time, and only the notes they share ring out together. When Qword plays a note Wyrd has no match for, Wyrd holds silence in its place: a left outer join.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Join me! (Inner join!)
Only where we match!
Join me! (Outer join!)
Keep the ones without a catch!
The left side and the right side together on the line,
Join me, join me, and your rows will meet mine!

songs.note: The most requested song of 1992. It is about tables.
songs.lesson: A join combines rows from two tables that match on a condition, usually a foreign key equal to a primary key. An inner join keeps only the rows that match on both sides. A left outer join keeps every row from the left table and fills in NULL where there’s no match. Leave out the condition and you get the cross product: every row paired with every other row.

songs.title: Group By

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A thousand rows of fan mail and I need to know the score,
How many from each city, and which city wrote me more?
Group them by the city, put the matching ones together,
Count them up in every pile, in fair and stormy weather!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Group by! (Count them up!)
Group by! (Sum them up!)
Count and sum and average, the smallest and the max,
Group by, and the totals are the facts!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Where filters every row before the groups are made,
Having filters groups after the totals have been weighed.
The average of a column or the total of a sale,
Aggregate the many into one and tell the tale!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Count! (How many?) Sum! (How much?)
Average! (How so?) Max! (How high can it go?)

parts.label: Drum solo: Bytes
parts.desc: Bytes plays scattered hits, then sorts them into clusters by drum: all the snares together, then the toms, then the cymbals. Each cluster ends with a single loud accent: its count.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Group by! (Count them up!)
Group by! (Sum them up!)
Count and sum and average, the smallest and the max,
Group by, and the totals are the facts!

songs.note: The crowd chant was recorded while counting the band’s fan mail, one bag at a time.
songs.lesson: Aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX summarize many rows into one value. GROUP BY splits rows into groups that share a value and aggregates each group. WHERE filters rows before they’re grouped, and HAVING filters the groups afterwards.

songs.title: Anomaly

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Four copies of the setlist and no two are the same,
I changed a song on my list, but yours still has the old name.
The same fact in four places, and I only fixed the one,
An update anomaly, and the show is coming undone!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Anomaly! (It’s not the same!)
Anomaly! (Who’s to blame?)
Store it twice and one day you’ll be wrong,
Anomaly, anomaly, in every song!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Can’t add a song we haven’t played, the table needs a show,
Delete the only show it’s in and the song is gone, you know.
Insert, update, delete, three ways to break the truth,
Redundancy’s the devil, and it’s been there since our youth!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Insert anomaly! (Can’t add!)
Delete anomaly! (Lost what we had!)
Update anomaly! (Changed in one place!)

parts.label: Out of sync: full band
parts.desc: Every member plays the same riff from their own copy of the chart, and every copy is slightly different. It falls apart in eight bars, the way the setlists did every night.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Anomaly! (It’s not the same!)
Anomaly! (Who’s to blame?)
Store it twice and one day you’ll be wrong,
Anomaly, anomaly, in every song!

songs.note: About the four setlists. Every night, somebody played the wrong song.
songs.lesson: Storing the same fact in more than one place causes anomalies. Update anomaly: you change one copy and the others go stale. Insertion anomaly: you can’t record one fact without an unrelated one. Deletion anomaly: removing one fact accidentally removes another. Normalization removes the redundancy that causes all three.

songs.title: Third Normal Form

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: First normal form, one value in each cell,
No lists inside a column, no repeating groups as well.
Second normal form, the whole key, not a part,
Every column hangs upon the whole key from the start!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: The key! (The key!) The whole key! (The whole key!)
And nothing but the key, so help me Codd!
Third normal form, every fact in its place,
Store it once and only once, and look it in the face!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Third normal form, no column leans upon another,
No fact that hangs upon a fact that hangs upon its brother.
Split the tables, link the keys, and every fact is stored
In exactly one place, and the anomalies are floored!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: One fact! (One place!)
One fact! (One place!)
Join it back together when you need to see its face!

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Qword plays one huge, tangled phrase, then splits it into three clean pieces, each played by only one instrument, and finally joins them back together. Nothing repeats, and nothing is lost.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: The key! (The key!) The whole key! (The whole key!)
And nothing but the key, so help me Codd!
Third normal form, every fact in its place,
Store it once and only once, and look it in the face!

songs.note: The title track. The chorus is an old database designer’s oath, and the band swears by it.
songs.lesson: First normal form: every cell holds a single value, with no lists or repeating groups. Second normal form: every non-key column depends on the whole key, not just part of it. Third normal form: no non-key column depends on another non-key column. The usual summary is “the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.” Split tables apart, link them by keys, and join them back together when you need to. Edgar Codd invented the relational model.

songs.title: Null

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: An empty space where the value should be,
Not zero, not blank, just a mystery.
Is it missing? Is it unknown? Nobody can say,
Null sits in the column and it won’t go away.

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Null! (Is it true?) Null! (Is it false?)
Neither one, it’s unknown, and it answers no calls!
Null equals null isn’t true, my friend,
Null is unknown from beginning to end!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: True and unknown is unknown, false and unknown is false,
Three-valued logic, three steps in the waltz.
Don’t ask if it equals null, ask if it is null instead,
Or the rows you’re looking for will never reach your head!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Is null! (Yes!) Equals null! (Unknown!)
Is null! (Yes!) Equals null! (Unknown!)

parts.label: The missing solo: no one
parts.desc: Four bars where the solo should be: no guitar, no drums, just one faint organ note so quiet you can’t tell if it’s really there. Not zero. Not nothing. Unknown.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Null! (Is it true?) Null! (Is it false?)
Neither one, it’s unknown, and it answers no calls!
Null equals null isn’t true, my friend,
Null is unknown from beginning to end!

songs.note: Null finally got a song. The band asked the duck whether it was equal to itself. The duck said nothing, which, according to the database, is the correct answer.
songs.lesson: NULL marks a missing or unknown value. It isn’t zero and it isn’t an empty string. SQL uses three-valued logic, so comparing anything with NULL gives UNKNOWN, which means NULL = NULL is not true, and WHERE only keeps rows that are TRUE. Test for it with IS NULL or IS NOT NULL. Most aggregates skip NULLs.

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: A million rows and I’m looking for one,
Read them all one by one and the night is done.
But build an index, a tree of the keys,
Jump down to the leaf and you’ll find it with ease!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Index! (Find it fast!)
Index! (Built to last!)
A tree of the keys and the search is short,
Index, index, a log n report!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: A B-tree is wide and its branches are low,
A few steps down and the record will show.
But every index costs you every time you write,
Index what you search for, not every column in sight!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Full table scan! (Slow!)
Index seek! (Go!)

parts.label: Lead guitar solo: Qword
parts.desc: Instead of walking up the neck one fret at a time, Qword jumps straight to the target note in three big leaps, each one narrowing the range. A full scan would have taken the whole song.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Index! (Find it fast!)
Index! (Built to last!)
A tree of the keys and the search is short,
Index, index, a log n report!

songs.note: Recorded in one take, because Bytes could always jump straight to his place in the song.
songs.lesson: Without an index, a query may have to read every row in the table, a full table scan. An index, usually a B-tree, keeps the keys sorted in a wide, shallow tree, so a lookup takes only a few steps. Indexes make reads faster but writes slower, and they take up space, so index the columns you actually search on.

songs.title: ACID

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Take the money from my account and put it into yours,
Halfway through, the power dies, and the money’s on the floors.
A transaction is all or nothing, it never stops halfway,
Atomic, all together, or it never saw the day!

parts.label: Chorus
lines: A! (Atomic!) C! (Consistent!)
I! (Isolated!) D! (Durable!)
ACID! Burning through the night!
ACID! Keep the data right!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Consistent from a valid state to another valid one,
Isolated, so the others never see it half done.
Two writers at the same time, and the locks will keep them straight,
No dirty reads, no lost updates, no one sees the in-between state!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: Begin! (Start it!) Rollback! (Undo it!)
Commit! (Prove it!)

parts.label: Organ and bass duet: Wyrd and Nyble
parts.desc: Wyrd and Nyble play a four-bar phrase that only counts if they both finish it. Twice, Bytes cuts them off with a crash halfway through, and they roll back to the start. The third time they make it all the way through: committed.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: A! (Atomic!) C! (Consistent!)
I! (Isolated!) D! (Durable!)
ACID! Burning through the night!
ACID! Keep the data right!

songs.note: The band’s only song with a chemistry warning on the sleeve. The warning is incorrect.
songs.lesson: A transaction groups several operations into one unit of work, with four guarantees known as ACID. Atomicity: all of it happens or none of it does. Consistency: it moves the database from one valid state to another. Isolation: transactions running at the same time don’t see each other’s half-finished work. Durability: once committed, changes survive crashes. BEGIN starts a transaction, COMMIT makes it permanent, and ROLLBACK undoes it.

songs.title: Commit

parts.label: Verse 1
lines: Four copies on the floor of the van,
Every one is different and none of them a plan.
So we wrote it down once, in a single place,
Every song a number, every number in its space.

parts.label: Chorus
lines: Commit! (And it’s written in the log!)
Commit! (Through the rain and through the fog!)
Once it’s committed, it survives the night,
Commit, commit, and the data’s right!

parts.label: Verse 2
lines: Write it to the log before you change the page,
If the power dies, the log replays it stage by stage.
Undo what wasn’t finished and redo what was done,
The database wakes up and every fact is one!

parts.label: Bridge
lines: One setlist! (One place!)
Every song! (By key!)
Every member reads the same, and that’s the way to be!

parts.label: Convergence: full band
parts.desc: The four members start the solo quietly, each playing a fragment of their own. Bar by bar they converge on one shared part, until all four are playing the same line, from the same chart, at full volume.

parts.label: Final chorus
lines: Commit! (And it’s written in the log!)
Commit! (Through the rain and through the fog!)
Once it’s committed, it survives the night,
Commit, commit, and the data’s right!

songs.note: The night they finished the album, the band threw away three of the four setlists and kept one. Everyone else refers to it by number.
songs.lesson: Durability is usually built with a write-ahead log: every change is written to the log before the data itself is updated. After a crash, the database replays the log, redoing committed transactions and undoing unfinished ones. Once a transaction is committed, it’s permanent.
